name: Indonesian
catalog_quote: Indonesian does not have word stress at all ... The domain of the accent is, by default, the phrase.
sweep_summary: indo1316 (Standard Indonesian) is in the catalog with deciding quote from Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 (pp.36, 56, held in full): no word stress, accent domain = phrase (the catalog_kind 'fixed-dominant' vs that quote is already flagged in the stin1234 audit record). Three sweep items, all about word stress in this language. (1) van Zanten, Goedemans & Pacilly 2003 (Benjamins, paywalled; Crossref/jbe-platform show no OA copy; Leiden repository and every search engine blocked from our machine): Google Books snippets of its conclusion — 'good reason to exclude the penultimate stress hypothesis... the rule that drives prominence patterns in the influential Javanese variety of Indonesian is phrasal... prominence may freely occur on any of the last two syllables (and sometimes even the antepenult) of any word... [Javanese variant] may have a phrasal accent only' — CONFIRM the catalog coding; it is the earlier (Jakartan-listener) report of the experiments written up in the held 2007 chapter (G&vZ 2007 fn.4 p.48), so it does not supersede the deciding source. (2) Odé & van Heuven (eds) 1994, Semaian 9 (HathiTrust search-only at Michigan, Google Books snippet view; no open copy): Laksman's chapter (pp.108-139) reports experimental penultimate stress in disyllabic words — p.133 'Stress was invariably perceived on the penultimate syllable. Therefore, I conclude that one of these two parameters (Fo and duration) characterizes the stress' — and that schwa can be stressed; on its own terms it CONTRADICTS the no-word-stress coding, but the same Leiden group later called that view 'no longer defensible' (van Heuven & van Zanten 2007: 194, held) and cites it only for 'schwa can be stressed'/'a tendency, not an absolute rule'. Medium priority to acquire the Laksman chapter (print: U Michigan, MPI-EVA). (3) Samsuri 1971 (Nusa Indah, Ende; paper from the 1968 Seminar Bahasa Indonesia; Google Books snippet view of the original-spelling booklet 3tlBAQAAIAAJ and the proceedings I4hbAAAAIAAJ): three degrees of stress (lemah/biasa/keras), stress non-phonemic ('tidak fonemis'; changing its position changes no meaning), and strong stress on the final syllable of words/phrases in isolation ('suku achir mendapat tekanan jang keras') — the 'final stress hypothesis' of the literature (G&vZ 2007: 39; vZ&G 2009: 198; Roosman 2007: 91); CONTRADICTS the catalog coding but is impressionistic and superseded; low priority. Best new statement = the 2003 conclusion (snippet-only), confirming, not superseding, the held 2007 deciding source. All receipts (Glottolog.bib, Crossref, HathiTrust bib API, OpenLibrary, 60+ Google Books GData snippet files) and copies of the held 2007/2009 Leiden texts are under with. the legacy Google Books GData feed and Glottolog.bib endpoints were the working channels.

new_statements.reading: Indonesian as spoken by the dominant Javanese-substrate speakers has no word-level stress; prominence is a phrasal accent that may land on either of the last two syllables (occasionally the antepenult) of the phrase-final word. This is the 2003 report (Jakartan listeners) of the same experiments whose 2007 write-up (Goedemans & van Zanten 2007: 36, 56, held in full) is the catalog's deciding source; it confirms that coding. Caveat: read only as Google Books snippet fragments stitched with ellipses, not as a continuous page; the held 2007 chapter says the same thing in full text.

audit.recode_to: Preferred: 'no word-level stress; phrase-level (right-edge) prominence' — i.e. move the row out of the word-pattern census (dominant set included), consistent with the record's own domain verdict REFUTED->LUMPED and with Goedemans & van Zanten 2007:36,56 (held), van Zanten & Goedemans 2009:197,213-214 (fetched sources), Athanasopoulou et al. 2021. Fallback if the catalog keeps a 'penult reading' row in the dominant set: primary-only penult, no secondary rhythm — 10 010 0010 00010 000010 0000010 00000010 — per Halim 1981:56,58, Lapoliwa 1981:31,128 ('only one degree of stress'), Soderberg & Olson 2008:211, Macdonald & Soenjono 1967:31; the coded initial+alternating secondaries (1010, 101010, 1001010...) rest on Cohn 1989's impressionistic data alone (Cohn & McCarthy 1994 fn.3). Either way, fill the empty quote/cite/loc (e.g. Cohn & McCarthy 1994 ROA-25 p.1 ex.(1) = Cohn 1989:170 for the StressTyp2 profile) and note the held sources sit under indo1316, not stin1234.

sources.note: Two perception experiments with Jakartan listeners (indirect native-speaker judgements of prominence placed on different syllables of Javanese-style and Toba-Batak-style stimuli). Conclusion: the penultimate-stress hypothesis is excluded; prominence in the influential Javanese variety of Indonesian is phrasal, may fall freely on either of the last two syllables (sometimes the antepenult), and is not a word-level phenomenon. sources.quote: p.56: 'Within a word there is one syllable which is accentuated. The accent which falls on this syllable is traditionally called word accent.' p.58: 'Notice that the accent placement in polysyllabic-base words is perfectly regular: the accent falls on the penultimate syllable.' (examples ístiméwa-type four- and five-syllable bases marked with a single accent on the penult; prefixes do not affect placement; instrumental chapter 3.1 finds pitch and duration as correlates)

sources.citation: Farinella, Alessa, Constantijn Kaland & Daniel Kaufman. 2025. Gesture, prosodic prominence and stresslessness in Indonesian. Language and Cognition 17: e92, 1-22. DOI 10.1017/langcog.2025.10043 (CC BY)
sources.quote: 'Early, impressionistic studies claimed that stress regularly occurs on the penultimate syllable, but shifts to the final syllable when the penult contains schwa (Cohn, 1989; Halim, 1981; Stoel, 2007)... However, recent work rejects the claim that Indonesian displays any evidence of regular word-level stress, claiming instead that the language is stressless (Athanasopoulou et al., 2021; Goedemans & van Zanten, 2014; Odé & van Heuven, 1994).' Own finding: gesture aligns to word-penult in eastern varieties (word-based) and to final syllables, phrase-based, in the Javanese variety.

Yet, we do observe some kind of prominence pattern.' pp.213-214: 'we must conclude that the Javanese variant of Indonesian does not have word stress... the data we have gathered in these experiments forcefully refute the claim that stress is penultimate in Indonesian... the most common and influential variant of Indonesian does not have stress at all.' sources.citation: Soderberg, Craig D. & Kenneth S. Olson. 2008. Indonesian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 38(2): 209-213. DOI 10.1017/S0025100308003320
sources.quote: 'Stress in Indonesian is predictable. Unaffixed words in isolation have primary stress on the penultimate syllable, but if the vowel in the penultimate syllable is a schwa /ə/, the stress usually occurs on the ultimate syllable (depending on the dialect).' Examples ˈpintu, ˈsampaj, bəˈlum, əˈmas; no secondary stress mentioned or transcribed.

sources.quote: [p.133, Laksman] "Stress was invariably perceived on the penultimate syllable. Therefore, I conclude that one of these two parameters (Fo and duration) characterizes the stress. The stress marking of words in a carrier-sentence is more or less reflected in final words of NPs positioned after the verb." [p.38, Odé's survey] "... the central vowel [ə] is always unaccented, we have found that it can be accented as well as all other vowels." In her conclusion Laksman states that, generally speaking, [in disyllabic words accent is realized in the penultimate ...] stress is still perceived in the penultimate syllable." [pp.38-40] "1. In isolation: word stress on the penultimate syllable, realized by pitch obtrusion in that syllable, even if the vowel is a pepet. 2. Before a verb: word stress on the penultimate syllable, realized by duration, even if there is pitch obtrusion in the final syllable or if the word is not (pitch-)accented. 3. After a verb: word stress on the penultimate syllable, realized by pitch obtrusion 'en finale de la phrase' (Laksman [n.d.]: 78)"
sources.locator: Laksman chapter p.133 (running head 'LOCATION OF STRESS 133'); Odé survey p.38 and the three-point summary of Laksman's earlier findings (pp. 38-40); all from Google Books snippet fragments
sources.note: The volume is mostly intonation (Cornell Phonetics Lab WP 1996 snippet: 'While the volume focuses primarily on intonation, Laksman (1994) is of direct relevance to the question of word stress'). Laksman's chapter reports a production/perception study of disyllabic words: stress was invariably perceived on the penultimate syllable, with F0 (in isolation) or duration (in context) as the correlate, and schwa (pepet) can carry it. Odé's survey (pp.39-41, per Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 fn.2) lists three hypotheses for Indonesian stress position (final: Samsuri 1971; penultimate; none). This 1994…
